content: Efforts to reduce the burden of diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs) include implementing public policies that foster food environments conducive to healthy diets and regulating private sector activities that influence health, known as the commercial determinants of health. However, the private sector continues to exert influence on public health policy and regulation through lobbying and other actions. Food marketing, particularly the promotion of foods high in fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS), has been recognized as having a particularly harmful impact on children’s diets. Marketing is a well-established method to promote products harmful to health, such as HFSS foods. Arguments defending such marketing lose credibility when the marketed products harm health and infringe on children’s rights. Modern marketing techniques, such as food-themed apps, influencer marketing, and user-generated content, raise additional concerns. These methods often involve the collection of extensive personal data from internet users, which is then used to target marketing efforts. Dietary risks include diets low in whole grains, fruits, nuts, seeds, vegetables, fiber, legumes, polyunsaturated fatty acids, calcium, or milk, and/or high in sodium, trans fats, processed meat, red meat, or sugary drinks. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines to protect children from the harmful effects of food marketing. These guidelines build on the 2010 WHO recommendations on the marketing of foods and non-alcoholic beverages to children. Since then, evidence of the harmful impact of food marketing has grown, but country-level action remains limited. Children continue to be exposed to marketing for HFSS foods, and new marketing media, such as digital platforms, have emerged as a growing concern. The definition of marketing in these guidelines is comprehensive, encompassing any form of commercial communication, message, or action designed to advertise or promote a product, service, or brand. This includes advertising, product placement, branding, sponsorship, direct marketing, product design, packaging, and point-of-sale marketing. Marketing is recognized as a significant driver of food environments that influence children’s dietary behaviors, ultimately affecting their weight status and risk of developing diet-related NCDs. The Convention on the Rights of the Child emphasizes children’s rights to health, adequate and nutritious food, privacy, and freedom from exploitation. Countries that are State Parties to the Convention have legal obligations to respect, protect, and fulfill these rights. This includes taking immediate action to protect children from marketing of HFSS foods, which negatively impacts their rights. The Committee on the Rights of the Child has called for the regulation of marketing for foods high in fat, sugar, or salt, particularly in the digital environment, to prevent children’s exposure to such marketing. Despite growing recognition of the harmful impact of food marketing on children, only 60 countries have adopted policies to restrict such marketing as of May 2022, and only 20 of these have mandatory policies. Existing measures often fail to cover all forms of marketing or adequately define the age of children protected by the policies. For example, most policies only cover children up to the age of 12. Additionally, while 93% of countries with restrictions include television marketing, only 29% address social media marketing. The WHO has developed this guideline to support Member States in creating and implementing policies to protect children from the harmful impact of food marketing. The guideline considers recent evidence on the effectiveness of policies to restrict food marketing and the evolution of new marketing media and techniques. It is not an implementation manual but provides recommendations on measures to take. Detailed implementation guidance can be found in the WHO/UNICEF publication Taking action to protect children from the harmful impact of food marketing: a child rights-based approach. The guideline aligns with other WHO recommendations, including those on sodium and sugar intake, and forthcoming guidelines on fats, carbohydrates, and non-sugar sweeteners. It emphasizes the need for a comprehensive package of policy actions to improve the food environment and enable healthy dietary practices among children. The target audience includes policymakers, health professionals, educators, and organizations involved in developing, implementing, and advocating for policies to restrict food marketing to children.
